newsitem.title: FRANCE: Credit Foncier Paris sit-in ends.
newsitem.headline: Credit Foncier Paris sit-in ends.

text.p: Employees of French bank Credit Foncier voted on Thursday to end their occupation of its Paris headquarters after a 21-day protest at government plans to dismember the property lender.
"We have decided to suspend the occupation as of this morning," a union spokesman said.

The action to end their protest followed the bank's decision on Wednesday to allow it to continue operations despite the hole in its books since reporting 1995 losses of 10.8 billion francs ($1.96 billion).
Several hundred staff occupied the downtown headquarters nearly three weeks ago in a battle to halt government plans for a partial takeover of the bank and a wind-down of the rest.
They held its chairman hostage for six days but the sit-in had been toned down in recent days in terms of numbers of people involved, and offices are open for business.

Staff were fighting a plan unveiled by Finance Minister Jean Arthuis in July which would involve spinning off Foncier's property loans business to cooperatively run Credit Immobilier and shunting the rest into a state holding company to be shut down over time.

Le Monde newspaper said a report by Paribas bank had confirmed the possibility of Foncier making a profit of more than one billion francs this year but said that it could need a recapitalisation of up to six billion francs.

Arthuis has already carried out the first stage of his plan by getting the state-owned bank Caisse des Depots et Consignations to "nationalise" Foncier through a buyout of shareholders for more than two billion francs.
Credit Foncier was private but had top management named by the state because of its status as a "specialised financial institution" providing low-cost home loans to France's poorer families.
Unions argue the losses were overstated.

Under Credit Foncier's statutes, which are different from those of ordinary companies, the 145-year-old bank should have plugged its balance sheet within four months and was able to stay in business only following the state-sponsored takeover.
But the bank on Wednesday passed a resolution altering its statutes so it could continue to run.
